questions.q: How does this lesson distinguish capacity planning from the Instance Health Dashboard monitoring taught in Performance Troubleshooting?
options: The Instance Health Dashboard cannot be used as a data source for capacity planning
Capacity planning and monitoring are two names for the exact same activity
Monitoring shows today's load; capacity planning projects the trend forward and sizes the platform ahead of where it's actually going
Capacity planning only applies to instances that are already overloaded
questions.explain: Capacity planning reuses the same underlying data but asks a forward-looking question: will today's configuration still hold up at next year's projected load?

questions.q: Why does this lesson treat user growth and data growth as two independent dimensions to track separately?
options: Semaphore pools are affected only by data volume, never by user count
They strain different parts of the platform — user growth strains node capacity and semaphore pools, data growth strains query performance and storage
User growth and data growth always happen at exactly the same rate
Only data growth has any real capacity impact on a ServiceNow instance
questions.explain: A rollout that triples users but leaves data flat carries a different capacity risk than one that triples data volume with flat user count — they need separate projections.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what should an architect do if concurrent usage is projected to double next year and the semaphore pool is already running near capacity today?
options: Ignore the projection since today's semaphore utilization is currently fine
Wait until users start reporting queuing delays before taking any action
Treat the coming contention as a near-certainty to plan for now, not a future possibility to just monitor for
Assume semaphore pools scale automatically as user count grows
questions.explain: This is the core proactive move: running the growth math forward against today's capacity before the queuing symptom that Performance Troubleshooting's diagnostic tools would otherwise have to find.

questions.q: What three example growth-tracking metrics does this lesson name as the basis for a real capacity plan?
options: Active user count by month, record count growth in core tables, and average/peak semaphore utilization
Total number of ServiceNow modules installed and their version numbers
Number of Business Rules written, number of UI Actions created, and number of client scripts deployed
The number of open incidents currently assigned to the platform team
questions.explain: These three concrete, trended figures — pulled from the Instance Health Dashboard — turn capacity planning into a data-driven discipline rather than guesswork.

questions.q: Why does this lesson emphasize a fixed review cadence for capacity metrics, rather than a one-time estimate made at project kickoff?
options: Quarterly reviews are required by ServiceNow's platform licensing terms
A recurring cadence catches a wrong projection early, while there's still time to act on it, rather than only noticing when things already feel slow
Capacity projections never need to be revisited once they're made
A review cadence is only useful for instances that have already experienced an outage
questions.explain: An ongoing review cadence is what makes capacity planning a discipline instead of a guess made once and never checked against real trend data.
